Angle Bisector In Equilateral Trapezoid

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Move the four corners of a trapezoid and the dot inside it, and watch when four new dots land on one circle.
How to play: Drag A, B, C, D or G with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press the middle-line button to see the special case.
Look for the math

This is problem 5 from the 2009 USA Mathematical Olympiad. Four new points are built from a trapezoid inside a circle. The surprise is that they lie on one circle precisely when one line at B cuts an angle exactly in half — move any point and the two events always happen together.

A trapezoid that fits a circle

The trapezoid ABCD has AB parallel to CD and all four corners on one circle. Such a cyclic quadrilateral must be isosceles: its two sloping sides are equal, AD = BC. The centre of the circle sits on the same middle line as the centres of both parallel sides, so reflecting one end of a base in that line gives the other end. The core uses this to keep the picture a true trapezoid after every drag, and the logic test checked it on hundreds of shapes.

How the four points are made

The point G lies inside triangle BCD. The line from A through G meets the circle again at P, and the line from B through G meets it again at Q. Through G draw a line parallel to AB: it meets BD at R and BC at S. That is all — the question is only when P, Q, R, S are concyclic.

When BG cuts the angle in half

Let BG split CBD into two equal parts. Then Q is the midpoint of the arc CD, so it lies directly above the circle's centre — this is exactly when the applet turns on its hint box, and the status line here says the hint is unlocked. Let T be where BQ meets CD. Triangles DTB and QCB are similar, which makes triangles DGB and QSB similar as well, so BDG = BQS. Equal inscribed angles give GPD = BDC = BRS, making DRGP cyclic; putting the equal angles together gives RQS = RPS, so PQRS is cyclic.

And only then

Conversely, assume PQRS is cyclic. Both ABPQ and RSPQ are cyclic, so AQR = BPS; with AQB = APB this gives BQR = SPG. Since GSC = GPC, the quadrilateral GSPC is cyclic and SPQ = SCG, hence BQR = BCG. If DBQ were bigger than CBQ, triangles BRQ and BGC would force BQ/BC > BD/BM by the sine rule, while triangles BDM and BCQ force the opposite inequality — a contradiction. The other case is the same argument reversed, so the two parts of CBD must be equal.

The logic test checks the whole "if and only if" on hundreds of random trapezoids: with G on the bisector the four points are cyclic to within 1e-7 of the circle's radius; with G clearly off it they are not. It also reproduces every constructed point from a second transcription of the applet's own bytecode.

Press Put G on the middle line, then drag A or B: the green circle through P, Q, R, S follows every change. Now drag G just a little away and watch the circle vanish.
